Various Ways to Define a Permutation

PermutationsCountingAlgebra
Game: A permutation shuffles the numbers 1 to N. See the same shuffle drawn as a table, as lines, upside down, as cycles and as a list of counts.
How to play: Press "Reset" for a new shuffle and choose how to draw it. Press a number to see where it goes.

Look for the math

A permutation of the numbers 1 to N is a one-to-one match of them with themselves. It can be written as the list {f(1), ..., f(N)}, as a two-row table, as lines joining the rows, or as a set of cycles.

Upside down

If the lower row is kept in the natural order and the upper row is rearranged so that all the lines are vertical, the upper row reads f-1(1), ..., f-1(N): it shows the inverse permutation. The test confirmed that the inverse of the inverse is the original for every permutation of up to 8 numbers.

Cycles

Follow one number: where it goes, where that goes, and so on, until you are back. These loops are the cycles, and every permutation is a product of cycles that share no numbers. For the page's example {5, 9, 1, 8, 2, 6, 4, 7, 3} they are (1 5 2 9 3)(4 8 7)(6).

A list that says it all

For each i, count the numbers bigger than i that stand to its left. This list of inversions, found by Marshall Hall, determines the permutation: write N, then put N-1 to its right or left according to its count, and so on. The last count is always 0, the one before it 0 or 1, and in general ai can be anything from 0 to N-i, independently, so there are 1·2·3·...·N = N! lists, as many as permutations. The test checked every permutation up to N = 8: all lists are different and each rebuilds its permutation.

A fair shuffle

"Reset" goes backwards through the list and swaps each place with a random earlier one (or itself). For N places that is N! sequences of choices; the test ran all of them for N up to 7, and each permutation comes out exactly once, so no shuffle is favoured.

Set N to 3 and press Reset until you have seen all 6 permutations. Which one is its own inverse and which two are inverses of each other?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
